deep.reconstruction:
Context. This page is part of Riemann's draft of his 1851 dissertation, around Arts. 15-17 of the table of contents on the next page. The topic is Dirichlet's principle for L = ∫(λ_x²+λ_y²) dT. The previous page argues that λ cannot approach, with L staying finite, a function σ that is discontinuous along a line. Near that line Riemann uses curvilinear coordinates: s is arc length along the line, p is the normal distance, and κ is the curvature. In these coordinates the area element is (1-κp) ds dp, so the contribution of a strip of T' to L is ∫ds ∫_{p2}^{p1}[(∂λ/∂p)² + (∂λ/∂s)²/(1-κp)²](1-κp) dp. Dropping the s-derivative term gives a lower bound.

Step 1 (one-dimensional minimisation). Fix s. Minimise J = ∫_{p2}^{p1} λ'(p)² (1-κp) dp with λ(p1)=λ1 and λ(p2)=λ2 fixed ('nach bekannten Regeln'). My fill-in:
- The Euler-Lagrange equation is ((1-κp)λ')' = 0, so λ' = c/(1-κp).
- Then λ1-λ2 = c∫_{p2}^{p1} dp/(1-κp) = (c/κ)[log(1-κp2) - log(1-κp1)].
- J_min = ∫ c²/(1-κp) dp = c(λ1-λ2) = (λ1-λ2)² κ / [log(1-κp2) - log(1-κp1)].
- As κ→0 this tends to (λ1-λ2)²/(p1-p2), the bound on the previous page.
- Hence the contribution of T' satisfies L_{T'} > ∫ (λ1-λ2)² κ ds / [log(1-κp2) - log(1-κp1)].

Step 2 (the bound blows up). As p1, p2 → 0 from the two sides, λ1-λ2 tends to the finite nonzero jump of σ. So one can choose P1 and P2 such that m = min (λ1-λ2)² > 0 for all p_i between 0 and P_i. Set α = ∫ mκ ds / D0, where D0 is the logarithmic denominator evaluated at P1, P2. Riemann requires, for every s, that each one-sided logarithm be at most α/C times its value at P_i. The conditions are 1-κp ≥ (1-κP)^{α/C} on each side, i.e. |p_i| below |1-(1-κP_i)^{α/C}|/κ. Then D ≤ (α/C)D0, so the integral exceeds C.

Conclusion: for a sufficiently thin T', the part of L coming from T' exceeds any given quantity, whatever λ is inside T'. So λ cannot converge to a function with a jump along a line while L stays finite.

Step 3 (point singularities). If σ has only removable ('hebbare') point discontinuities, the region where σ and λ differ can shrink to nothing with L finite. Riemann's example is σ = (log 1/ρ)^α with α < 1/2. Check (mine): |∇σ|² = α²(log 1/ρ)^{2α-2}/ρ². Then ∫|∇σ|² dT = 2πα² ∫ (log 1/ρ)^{2α-2} dρ/ρ = 2πα² ∫^∞ t^{2α-2} dt, which is finite iff α < 1/2. So σ has finite Dirichlet integral but is unbounded at the point.

Consequence: the theorem of the previous article is modified. The minimum of Ω is attained, not necessarily by one of the admissible λ, but by a function with at most a removable discontinuity. This matches item 15 of the table of contents.

Step 4 (begun). Prescribing λ = 0 on the boundary and λ = a at an interior point O' does not prevent L from being made arbitrarily small. The construction starts with a fixed circle of radius 1 around O' and breaks off. Presumably (my fill-in) λ = a·log(1/ρ)/log(1/r) for r<ρ<1, λ = a for ρ ≤ r, and λ = 0 outside. Its energy is 2πa²/log(1/r) → 0. In modern terms, a point has zero capacity in the plane.
errors: The sign/index convention for p1, p2 is switched within the page. Earlier the text has P1>p1>0 and P2<p2<0 with denominator log(1-κp2)-log(1-κp1). Later the denominators are written log(1-κp1)-log(1-κp2) and the final inequalities have 0>p1, 0<p2. The final inequalities are internally consistent with the swapped convention (p1<0<p2), but the page mixes the two. This is a harmless notational slip.

α is written as ∫mκ ds divided by a log difference that depends on s through κ(s). Strictly it should be α = ∫ mκ ds/[log difference at P] with the denominator inside the integral. As literally written, the claimed inequality needs that reading.
The step uses 1-κp > 0 on T' (curvature centres outside the strip), as assumed on the previous page. It is not restated here.
The minimisation 'nach bekannten Regeln' is stated without proof, and minimality is only asserted. It is correct: the functional is convex.

results.what: Minimum of ∫_{p2}^{p1} (1-κp)λ'(p)² dp with fixed endpoint values equals (λ1-λ2)²κ/[log(1-κp2)-log(1-κp1)]. This is the energy of a radial harmonic (logarithmic) profile in an annular strip.
results.modern_name: 1D Euler-Lagrange minimisation; energy of the harmonic profile in an annulus (condenser capacity)

results.what: A function with a jump along a curve cannot be approximated with bounded Dirichlet integral by functions differing from it only in a shrinking neighbourhood of the curve.
results.modern_name: Functions with jumps across curves are not in H^1 (trace / jump argument)
results.usually_credited_to: standard in Sobolev space theory (20th c.); the Dirichlet-principle setting is Riemann 1851

results.what: σ = (log 1/ρ)^α with α<1/2 has finite Dirichlet integral although unbounded at a point. Hence finite energy does not exclude point singularities, and the minimiser may only be determined up to removable point discontinuities.
results.modern_name: Unbounded W^{1,2} function in dimension 2 (failure of Sobolev embedding into L^∞ / continuous functions at the critical exponent)
results.usually_credited_to: folklore of Sobolev space theory (1930s onward); similar log-log examples are standard textbook material

results.what: Prescribing the value at a single interior point does not bound the Dirichlet integral from below: L can be made arbitrarily small (construction started, cut off).
results.modern_name: Points have zero (Newtonian/logarithmic) capacity in the plane; failure of Dirichlet problem at isolated boundary points
results.usually_credited_to: Zaremba (1911) and Lebesgue (1913) for the Dirichlet-problem phenomenon; capacity theory later

deep.surprise_reason: The jump-line argument belongs to Riemann's known Dirichlet-principle work in the dissertation drafts. Less expected is the explicit unbounded finite-energy example (log 1/ρ)^α with α<1/2, together with the remark that a point constraint does not bound L from below (zero capacity of points). Both anticipate standard 20th-century Sobolev/capacity facts and points later raised in criticisms of Dirichlet's principle. However, they are unpublished draft remarks, and parts of this draft material are discussed in the Riemann literature.

checkable.sympy: p,k,c,p1,p2,l1,l2=symbols('p k c p1 p2 l1 l2',positive=True); lam=-c/k*log(1-k*p); simplify(diff((1-k*p)*diff(lam,p),p))
checkable.asserts: λ' = c/(1-κp) solves the Euler-Lagrange equation ((1-κp)λ')'=0 (result 0).
As κ→0 the bound reduces to (λ1-λ2)²/(p1-p2), the straight-line case on the previous page.
Dirichlet integral of (log 1/ρ)^α near ρ=0 (t = log 1/ρ) is finite for α=1/3<1/2; it diverges for α≥1/2.
Cut-off logarithmic function with value A at ρ≤r and 0 at ρ=1 has energy 2πA²/log(1/r), which tends to 0 as r→0 (point has zero capacity).
At the threshold p=(1-(1-κP)^{α/C})/κ the one-sided log term equals exactly α/C times its value at P (result 0, for 0<κP<1).

transcription_corrections: 'Function γ' (twice) is very likely 'Function σ' in Riemann's hand, consistent with σ on the previous page.
'jener Zuwachs': the word may be 'Beitrag' (the previous page speaks of 'den Beitrag'); uncertain from the image.

The denominator in the definition of α and in the final inequality reads log(1-κP_1)-log(1-κP_2) / log(1-κp_1)-log(1-κp_2), opposite in order to the first formula. This is faithful to the manuscript and should not be 'corrected'.
'hebbaren' is a plausible but uncertain reading. It agrees with 'hebbare Unstetigkeiten' in item 15 of the next page's table of contents.
